::: {.chapter-lead}
The previous page, [GPT and Transformers: architecture and data flow](transformer.qmd), places self-attention within the network's forward pass. We now start with a simple question: how can one position use the context provided by the other tokens?
:::

## The problem: using context

In “The cat chased the dog because it was fast,” the pronoun **it** could refer to either the cat or the dog. A model therefore cannot always interpret a token from its local representation alone: it needs to use information carried by other positions in the sequence.

That is what self-attention provides. For each position, the mechanism builds two things: **where to look** in the context and **what information to bring back**. Q, K, and V provide the representations needed for these two operations.

This example is adapted from [Neha KK](https://medium.com/@nkk18072004/understanding-queries-keys-and-values-in-transformers-149ed07c9f8b). It motivates the need for context; it does not prove that one isolated head resolves coreference or describe the attention weights of a trained model.

<div class="epistemic-badges">
  <span class="epistemic-badge badge-concept">Verified concept</span>
  <span class="epistemic-badge badge-status">Architecture: Transformer</span>
</div>

## Three complementary roles

The three projections are easiest to distinguish by following the flow of information:

- **Q — the query:** what the current position is looking to match in the context;
- **K — the key:** the representation that lets a position participate in the compatibility calculation;
- **V — the value:** the information carried by that position and available to be transmitted.

Q and K therefore determine **how attention is distributed**. V supplies **the content that is aggregated** using that distribution. A key is not a readable label, and a value is not a ready-made answer: they are learned numerical vectors.

![Diagram of query, key, and value projections: Q and K determine attention weights, which are used to aggregate V.](../images/queries-keys-values-en.svg){fig-alt="Two paths start from the same input: the Q and K vectors are compared to compute attention weights; those weights are then applied to V vectors to produce an aggregated representation." width=100%}

The diagram reveals two paths: one determines the weighting, the other supplies the content. **Why are three distinct projections needed to build these two paths from the same input?**

## Why three projections from the same input?

In self-attention, Q, K, and V are three learned transformations of the same representation stream. $X$ denotes the input to the attention sublayer: in the first block it starts from token embeddings; in later blocks it is an already contextualized hidden state. Positional information may be added upstream ([positional embeddings](positional-encoding.qmd)) or incorporated into queries and keys, as with [RoPE](rope.qmd).

For a sequence of $T$ positions, write $X\in\mathbb{R}^{T\times d_{model}}$:

$$
\begin{aligned}
Q &= XW_Q,\\
K &= XW_K,\\
V &= XW_V.
\end{aligned}
$$

The matrices $W_Q$, $W_K$, and $W_V$ are **distinct but learned jointly**. They let the model build, from the same input, representations suited to two different functions: computing compatibility (Q and K) and carrying content (V). This parameterization follows [Vaswani et al. (2017), *Attention Is All You Need*](https://arxiv.org/abs/1706.03762).

With $W_Q,W_K\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{model}\times d_k}$ and $W_V\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{model}\times d_v}$, the outputs have these shapes:

- $Q,K\in\mathbb{R}^{T\times d_k}$;
- $V\in\mathbb{R}^{T\times d_v}$.

Each row corresponds to one position. The same projection matrices are applied at every position, while the input representations vary. The dimensions $d_k$ and $d_v$ need not be equal; optional biases are omitted here. To trace these projections in the block implementation, see the [guided Transformer-block walkthrough](transformer-block-walkthrough.qmd); general dimension and axis conventions are covered in the [tensor reference](tensors.qmd).

## Further depth

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Another perspective: viewing Q and K in vector space"}
Codefinity offers a geometric intuition: picture Q and K as vectors whose orientation and alignment contribute to a compatibility score. This helps bridge conceptual roles and numerical objects.

For two vectors, the dot product can be written as:

$$
q^\top k = \lVert q\rVert\,\lVert k\rVert\cos(\theta).
$$

The angle is only part of the score: **the dot product also depends on the norms** of Q and K. It is not, in general, cosine similarity. This intuition is a bridge to the [scaled dot-product attention calculation](scaled-dot-product-attention.qmd), not a substitute for its mathematical definition.

Source: [Codefinity, *Queries, Keys, and Values: The Building Blocks*](https://codefinity.com/courses/v2/e7ee0772-6b82-4a1c-96ba-69b85ddee608/7ce26687-f7a7-4728-be33-7014c6c7b707/a5ac1dbf-dbec-4dd1-a8d6-f3d83cbb905b).
:::



::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="How does training learn these projections?"}
The matrices $W_Q$, $W_K$, and $W_V$ do not each receive an explicit “correct” target. They are adjusted indirectly from the model's loss function through backpropagation.

In the attention path considered here:

- the gradient reaching **Q and K** passes through the compatibility scores and the softmax that normalizes them;
- the gradient reaching **V** passes through the weighted aggregation: it indicates how the transmitted content contributes to the final error.

For a fixed input $X$, with no bias and the linear projections written above, the derivative rule has the form:

$$
\frac{\partial\mathcal L}{\partial W_Q}
=X^\top\frac{\partial\mathcal L}{\partial Q},
\qquad
\frac{\partial\mathcal L}{\partial W_K}
=X^\top\frac{\partial\mathcal L}{\partial K},
\qquad
\frac{\partial\mathcal L}{\partial W_V}
=X^\top\frac{\partial\mathcal L}{\partial V}.
$$

These gradients are computed in the context of the full network, and the optimizer then updates the parameters. The three projections are therefore **parameterized separately but learned jointly**: changing one can alter the output, while the other parameters also adapt during training. This explains the principle; it does not replace the full derivation of attention or backpropagation.
:::
::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Scope: the standard formulation and its variants"}
This page presents the standard formulation with separately parameterized Q, K and V projections. It is a useful baseline, not a claim that every Transformer uses three wholly independent projection matrices or the same number of query and key/value heads.

For example, **multi-query attention (MQA)** and **grouped-query attention (GQA)** use fewer key/value heads than query heads, sharing each key/value head across multiple query heads to reduce inference-time [KV-cache](llm-computational-complexity.qmd) costs. Other recent work studies tying projection parameters, including sharing the key and value projections. These are architecture variants with empirical trade-offs; they do not invalidate the role distinction taught here.



**Cross-attention:** in cross-attention, Q comes from the stream doing the querying, while K and V come from the stream being queried. The three projections therefore no longer share a common input stream. See the [advanced cross-attention lesson](cross-attention.qmd).
- Vaswani et al. (2017), [*Attention Is All You Need*](https://arxiv.org/abs/1706.03762) — standard Transformer attention formulation.
- Ainslie et al. (2023), [*GQA: Training Generalized Multi-Query Transformer Models from Multi-Head Checkpoints*](https://arxiv.org/abs/2305.13245) — grouped key/value heads.
- Kayyam et al. (2026), [*Do Transformers Need Three Projections? Systematic Study of QKV Variants*](https://proceedings.mlr.press/v306/kayyam26a.html) — empirical study of projection sharing.
:::



::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Another example: lexical ambiguity"}
Another case is lexical ambiguity: in “He sat by the bank,” with a river context, *bank* may mean a riverbank or a financial institution. This example from [Codefinity](https://codefinity.com/courses/v2/e7ee0772-6b82-4a1c-96ba-69b85ddee608/7ce26687-f7a7-4728-be33-7014c6c7b707/a5ac1dbf-dbec-4dd1-a8d6-f3d83cbb905b) illustrates another task to which contextualized representations may contribute. It does not show that one isolated attention head performs lexical disambiguation: no model, head, or measured weights are provided. An attention map alone is also insufficient to explain a model decision.

For the broader role of context in representations, see [Contextualized representations](contextualized-representations.qmd).
:::

## Takeaway and next steps

The functional distinction is simple but fundamental:

- **Q and K** determine compatibility scores, then attention weights;
- **V** supplies the vectors combined using those weights;
- changing V alone therefore leaves the weights unchanged, even though the aggregated content may change.

The weights are not a universal measure of semantic relevance, and attention is not nearest-neighbour search in the initial embedding space: it operates on learned projections.

The next lesson, [Scaled dot-product attention](scaled-dot-product-attention.qmd), explains how scores become weights and how those weights aggregate V. The [Attention exercises](exercises.qmd#attention) then let you manipulate the projections and verify these dependencies; numerical calculations remain in that practice route.

::: {.callout-note .learning-outcomes collapse="true" title="Learning outcomes"}
By the end of this lesson, you should be able to:
- distinguish the roles of Q, K, and V in the attention mechanism;
- explain why Q and K determine the weights while V supplies the aggregated content;
- describe the qualitative dependencies between projections, weights, and content, without performing matrix calculations.
:::

::: {.self-check}
## Check the essential idea

[Extended exercises on Q/K/V and attention](exercises.qmd#attention).

**Which projections determine attention weights, and which one supplies the aggregated vectors? What happens if V changes while Q and K stay the same?**

<details>
<summary>Show the reasoning</summary>

Q and K determine the attention weights; V supplies the vectors whose content is aggregated. Changing Q or K can change the weights. If only V changes, the weights remain unchanged because the scores depend on Q and K; the aggregated content can change, but need not do so: weighted changes can cancel out.

</details>
:::
